content: External resource persons are external experts who were invited to participate in the meetings of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health. Their involvement was based on specific tasks and roles, such as authorship of systematic reviews, provision of additional data and information as subject matter experts, expertise in methodologies and GRADE, or offering practical guidance on the implications of proposed recommendations. These individuals contributed to discussions on evidence review but did not have voting rights during the formulation of recommendations at NUGAG meetings. The final wording and determination of the strength of the recommendations were solely based on the consensus of NUGAG members. There was no formal requirement to assess the declaration of interests of these external resource persons. However, for transparency and record-keeping purposes, their declared interests are summarized below: 1. Dr. Janice Albert, Dr. Sarah Kelly, and Dr. Lisa Te Morenga declared no conflicts of interest. 2. Professor Ingeborg Brouwer disclosed that she assisted Dr. Martin Katan in preparing an expert witness report for the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in Sydney, Australia, regarding the health effects of conjugated linoleic acids (CLA) in the case of Cognis versus FSANZ. She declined financial compensation for this work. 3. Professor Francesco Cappuccio declared that he provided expert testimony on salt and cardiovascular disease (CVD) as part of the Guidance Development group of the UK’s National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) in 2009. He is an unpaid member of several organizations, including the Consensus Action on Salt and Health (2000–present), World Action on Salt and Health (WASH) (2003–present), National Heart Forum (2010–present), Pan American Health Organization/WHO Salt Group (2009–2011), and the European Salt Action Group (2007–present). 4. Professor Russell de Souza disclosed that he was a co-applicant on an investigator-initiated, unrestricted research grant provided by Coca-Cola to Dr. David Jenkins (his co-supervisor at St. Michael’s Hospital, Toronto, Canada) for conducting systematic reviews on fructose and CVD risk. Some funds from this grant were used to reimburse his travel to a scientific meeting in Canada unrelated to trans-fatty acids. 5. Professor Paul Elliott declared that he is a member of WASH. He also disclosed that his university is receiving research funds for the INTERMAP study from the US National Institutes of Health and that he received research support for a sodium intake study from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in 2010. He provided expert opinions on population sodium intake to the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey Sodium Working Group in January 2011 and on sodium intake measurement methods and efficacy to the CDC’s Epidemiology and Surveillance Branch during 2010–2011. 6. Dr. Cho-il Kim disclosed that in 2009, she provided expert opinion to the Korean Food and Drug Administration (KFDA) during the development of guidelines to identify energy-dense and nutrient-poor foods under the Special Act on Food Safety Management for Children. Since 2009, the sale of such foods has been prohibited within school premises and designated stores near schools (referred to as the Green Food Zone). Since 2010, television advertisements for these foods have been prohibited between 5:00 PM and 7:00 PM daily. Dr. Kim considered this information relevant because the regulations address the fat and sugar content of foods, which aligns with the NUGAG Subgroup’s review of recommendations on total fat and sugars. 7. Professor Ronald Mensink disclosed that he served as an adviser to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition, and Allergies (NDA) for the Dietary Reference Values for Fats, published on 25 March 2010. He also advised the Food, Nutrition, and Quality Sub-committee of the Malaysian Palm Oil Board (a government agency) during 2011–2013, receiving €800 annually, which was paid to his research unit (NUTRIM). Additionally, he received research support for the following projects: Research on cardiovascular risk markers (Feb 2011–Sept 2015) funded by the Top Institute for Food and Nutrition (TIFN), a public-private partnership. Research on the short-term effects of palm oil-derived diacylglycerol (DAG) on postprandial lipid and glucose metabolism in overweight and slightly obese men (Jan 2010–Dec 2010) funded by Sime Darby. Research on the effects of triacylglycerol structure of palmitic acid-rich fats on postprandial changes in lipid and glucose metabolism (April 2009–April 2011) funded by the Malaysian Palm Oil Board. Research on the effects of dairy products on metabolic risk markers in subjects with metabolic syndrome (Sept 2007–June 2011) funded by the Dutch Dairy Organization. 8. Professor Paula Moynihan disclosed that she received a research grant (to her university) that included reviewing sugar intake in care homes as a small component of a larger dietary study funded by the UK Food Standards Agency/Department of Health. The study was completed in January 2011. External Peer Reviewers: 1. Professor Annie S. Anderson, Dr. Jenny Reid, Professor W. Murray Thomson, and Dr. Paula R. Trumbo declared no conflicts of interest. 2. Professor Wulf Becker disclosed that he is employed by the Swedish National Food Agency and served as the chair of the working group responsible for producing the 5th edition of the Nordic Nutrition Recommendations (NNR 2012), a project financed by the Nordic Council of Ministers. His declared interests were not considered to constitute a conflict of interest for his role as an external peer reviewer for the guideline. Instead, his role as chair of the NNR 2012 working group was deemed important for critically reviewing the WHO guideline to ensure synergy between Sweden’s dietary guidance and global recommendations. 3. Dr. Hasan Hutchinson disclosed that he is the focal point for public health nutrition in Health Canada and presents healthy eating guidance to various stakeholders, including municipal, provincial, and national governments, NGOs, health professionals, academics, and industries. His declared interests were not considered to constitute a conflict of interest for his role as an external peer reviewer for the guideline. Instead, his role as the focal point for public nutrition in Canada was deemed important for critically reviewing the WHO guideline to ensure alignment between Canada’s dietary guidance and global recommendations.
